summary: Describes the extensions to CR-LDP signaling needed to support Generalized MPLS, which broadens the MPLS control plane to time-division, wavelength and spatial switching, such as in SONET, SDH and optical networks.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC extends Constraint-based Routed Label Distribution Protocol (CR-LDP) for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS). It adds message fields for paths through packet, time-division, wavelength, and fiber-switched links.

subtitle: CR-LDP signaling extensions for setting up MPLS paths across packet, optical, and fiber-switched links.

tldr.problem: MPLS signaling was designed around packet links, while Generalized MPLS also needs to set up paths through time-division, wavelength, and fiber switching.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3472 adds CR-LDP message fields and procedures for generalized labels, label restrictions, two-way paths, protection, administrative state, and data-interface identification.
tldr.outcome: It specifies the CR-LDP side of GMPLS signaling. RFC 3472 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 3468 and RFC 4201.

today: RFC 3472 is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 3468 and RFC 4201. The RSVP-TE version of these extensions is RFC 3473.

sections.title: GMPLS Signaling over CR-LDP
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) extends MPLS beyond packet switching. It also covers time-division multiplexing, lambda switching, and fiber switching. RFC 3471 describes the shared functions; RFC 3472 defines how to signal them with Constraint-based Routed Label Distribution Protocol (CR-LDP).

A separate specification, RFC 3473, defines corresponding extensions for RSVP-TE. The two signaling systems differ in failure handling: CR-LDP propagates detected failures outward with RELEASE and WITHDRAW messages, releasing resources and possibly returning resource information to the source.
sections.plainLanguage: Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) lets a network set up paths through more than packet links. This RFC explains the messages used when that setup uses Constraint-based Routed Label Distribution Protocol (CR-LDP).

sections.title: Requests, Labels, and Label Sets
sections.content:
A Generalized Label Request TLV tells downstream nodes the requested LSP encoding, switching type, and payload identifier. Nodes check that the incoming interface, node, and outgoing interface or tunnel can support those values. They report unsupported parameters with a NOTIFICATION.

A Generalized Label returns upstream in a MAPPING message. A Label Set can limit downstream label choices by adding or excluding individual labels or ranges. If a node cannot choose an allowed label, it terminates the request and sends a routing-problem notification. Waveband labels have start and end values; a node must swap these when a waveband switch mirrors wavelengths.
sections.plainLanguage: A request describes the kind of path that can work, and the reply identifies the label chosen for it. A label set can rule out labels that a link cannot use.

sections.title: Bidirectional Paths and Label Errors
sections.content:
An Upstream Label in a REQUEST marks a bidirectional Label Switched Path (LSP). The label must already be valid for forwarding when the request is sent. Each receiving node checks it; an intermediate node also allocates its outgoing label and establishes its internal data path before forwarding the request.

If the label is unacceptable or resources cannot be allocated, the node sends a NOTIFICATION. A notification can optionally include an Acceptable Label Set to suggest labels that would work. When the bidirectional LSP is removed, both labels become invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: A two-way path needs a label for traffic in each direction. Each router checks and prepares its part before passing the setup request along.

sections.title: Explicit Labels and Link Protection
sections.content:
A Label ER-Hop adds a specific label to an explicit route. It follows the route hop that identifies the link, and up to two may be present for a bidirectional LSP. A node copies a downstream label into a Label Set or an upstream label into an Upstream Label, then removes the label ER-Hop before forwarding.

An optional Protection TLV describes requested protection attributes. A transit node checks whether its outgoing interface or tunnel can meet them. If it cannot, it sends a NOTIFICATION reporting unsupported link protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can request a particular label on a particular link. It can also ask for link protection, which each transit router must check against its available link.

sections.title: Administrative State and Data Interfaces
sections.content:
The optional Admin Status TLV carries an LSP's administrative state in REQUEST and MAPPING messages, or requests a state change in a NOTIFICATION. Nodes update local state and pass the information along. The RFC also defines deletion procedures using the Delete bit; if a requested LABEL RELEASE does not arrive within the configurable wait, which defaults to 30 seconds, the node should release downstream and withdraw upstream.

When control and data channels are separate, an Interface ID TLV identifies the data interface. The request sender chooses the interface, and a receiving node returns the identifiers in its MAPPING. Nodes check consistency with the explicit route. For signaling-channel failures, recovery must preserve connection integrity at both ends.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can pass along an administrative status before removing a path. When signaling travels separately from data, the request also names the interface that carries the data.

sections.title: Security and Assigned TLVs
sections.content:
The RFC states that it adds no security considerations beyond the base CR-LDP specification, RFC 3212. It uses the LDP name spaces and assigns TLV types for generalized labels, label sets, status, interface identifiers, protection, and related information.

These assignments let CR-LDP messages identify each added piece of information. The RFC gives the assigned values in its IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says its security considerations are covered by the base CR-LDP specification. It also assigns distinct TLV types to the new signaling information.
